title: Emergency Reroute and Observability Handbook for Routing Modes
content:
Purpose:
This note captures our recommended monitoring signals, trigger thresholds, and step-by-step emergency reroute runbooks for incidents that require moving traffic between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private routing surfaces. It is targeted at platform engineers, on-call SREs, and the incident commander during multi-region or tenant-isolation events.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to inference request routing (control plane + data plane) for user-facing API traffic. Not covering batch offline jobs.
- Assumes tenants can be mapped to routing policies: hosted-default, dedicated-reserved, private-vpc.
- Focus is on graceful evacuation, minimum customer-visible error, and preserving isolation guarantees for Private deployments.

High-level goals during a routing incident:
1) Minimize user-visible 5xx/timeout errors across tenants.
2) Preserve contractual isolation for Private tenants (never route private traffic through hosted public pools).
3) Provide fast fallbacks for Dedicated when capacity or regional health degrades.
4) Maintain auditability — every reroute step must be recorded with reason, ticket, and rollback criteria.

Observability signals to watch (primary):
- Control plane health: api-controlplane-p95-latency, controlplane-errrate-1m, config-sync-lag.
- Serving runtime: per-pool p99 generation latency, token-throttle-rate, eviction-rate, gpu-utilization-per-node.
- Tenant-level: tenant-error-rate-5m, tenant-p95-latency-5m, tenant-fallback-count.
- Networking/region: egress-error-rate, cross-region-dns-failures, loadbalancer-503s.
- Safety/authorization: auth-fail-rate (to detect IAM/KMS problems when moving Private tenants).

Early warning thresholds (examples to tune per-customer SLA):
- controlplane-errrate-1m > 0.5% for 2 consecutive minutes => page platform oncall (P2).
- per-pool p99 latency increases > 2x baseline and sustained for 3 minutes => create incident, evaluate reroute.
- tenant-error-rate-5m > 1% for VIP tenants OR > 3% for standard tenants => notify customer-success and consider per-tenant mitigation.

Pre-approved mitigation patterns (ordered from least invasive):
A) Autoscale burst: allow Dedicated pool to temporarily scale above reserved capacity if autoscale budget available.
B) Prefix KV cache warmup: enable aggressive KV cache prefetch for hot tenants to reduce token cost and latency.
C) Shard-level throttling: apply token rate-limit to high-noise tenants.
D) Fallback to alternative model variant with lower resource usage (e.g., quantized variant) for best-effort customers.
E) Emergency reroute: move route to a compatible pool (hosted or alternate-region dedicated) — see below.

Emergency reroute decision matrix (simplified):
- If Dedicated pool under resource exhaustion but control plane healthy: attempt autoscale (A) then fallback to alternate Dedicated in same region.
- If Dedicated pool control plane degraded or region network failure: reroute to Hosted only if tenant is not Private and tenant policy allows (no private-data constraint).
- If Private tenant shows control plane or network failure: do NOT reroute to Hosted. Prefer on-prem standby or notify customer for manual intervention.
- If Hosted region has degradations across many tenants: shift some dedicated tenants to other dedicated regions (regional affinity spillover) before increasing hosted traffic.

Runbook: Emergency reroute from Dedicated -> Hosted (for eligible tenants)
1) Triage and ticket: create incident in PROD-9876, assign incident commander. Record initial signal snapshots (metrics links).
2) Verify policy: confirm tenant routing policy permits hosted failover (check tenant config). If not permitted, abort and follow Private path.
3) Capacity check: query hosted capacity pool for compatible model and region (api: /capacity/query). Confirm expected p99 after shift.
4) Notify stakeholders: post summary to #platform-incident and to affected customers (CS templated message).
5) Canary move: pick 1–2 low-latency, low-throughput tenants for canary reroute (5–10% traffic). Update routing table with TTL=30s and enable verbose logging.
6) Monitor 0–3 minutes: watch tenant-p95, tenant-error-rate. If errors < threshold, proceed. If errors spike, rollback immediately.
7) Gradual shift: incrementally increase % traffic to hosted pools in 10–20% steps until 100% or until capacity target reached.
8) Post-mortem metadata: annotate routing change with incident id, reason, and start/end times. Collect traces for 1 hour after cut.

Runbook: Emergency reroute for Private tenant (when Private control plane unreachable)
- Never route private tenant to hosted public pools. Our options are limited:
  * Attempt local reconnection: verify customer VPN/VPC peering, BGP session, and KMS connectivity.
  * Activate on-prem standby if configured (documented in tenant -> onprem-standby field).
  * If onprem-standby not present and outage is prolonged, engage account and legal for contract discussion.

Cross-region fallback: Dedicated region->Dedicated region
- Prefer same-cloud different-az within same region first (lower latency). If whole-region problem, route to geographically closest compatible dedicated region (respecting data residency).
- Apply affinity window: keep sticky routing for 30 minutes to allow KV caches to populate; use adaptive TTLs for subsequent requests.

Safety and controls (must-haves before any automated reroute):
- Reroute must be gated by a control plane action that is auditable (change recorded in controlplane mutation log with incident id).
- Feature flags: allow-automatic-reroute (global) and tenant-allow-fallback (per-tenant). If either disabled, reroutes require manual approval.
- Quotas: ensure hosted fallback respects tenant usage caps to prevent billing surprises.

Tooling checklist for on-call (quick commands):
- Check pool health: infractl pool status --pool dedicated-us-west-1 --json
- Query tenant policy: infractl tenant get --tenant-id T-12345
- Propose reroute (dry run): infractl routing plan --from dedicated-us-west-1 --to hosted-us-west-1 --tenant T-12345 --dry-run
- Apply reroute: infractl routing apply --plan-id PLAN-6789 --incident PROD-9876
- Rollback: infractl routing rollback --incident PROD-9876 --to previous

Observability improvements we should prioritize (next quarter):
- Per-tenant synthetic checks with lightweight inference probes (detect early model-level regressions).
- End-to-end trace linking from API request through control plane routing decision to serving runtime execution (reduce triage time).
- Automated impact predictor: before applying reroute, simulate expected p99 using a short probe run and return confidence score.

Open questions / risks:
- How to handle billing reconciliation when hosted fallback increases usage on hosted pools (chargeback vs free during incident)?
- Private tenants with BYOK and KMS constraints sometimes block even intra-cloud fallback; we need clearer customer onboarding docs to set expectations.
- Potential for cascading failures if many tenants fallback to hosted at once; need global circuit-breaker heuristics.

Appendix: short incident checklist (one-pager to paste into chat):
- page: platform-oncall
- create incident and record signals
- confirm tenant policy (allow-fallback?)
- capacity check on destination pool
- canary 5–10% traffic move, observe 3m
- ramp in steps, monitor p95/p99 and error-rate
- annotate and close incident with post-mortem links

Notes to self / drafting fragments:
- Consider a small internal SLA that states: "Hosted fallback for non-private tenants may be used during region-level failures; customers will be notified and billed normally unless credits are approved."
- Add a templated customer communication for fallback in the CS playbook.
- Follow-up: meet with security to validate that hosted fallback does not violate SOC2 scopes for any flagged customers.

End of handbook.
